Name: shared_negation_operator
Title: One 'Not' to Rule Them All? Testing Whether Multilingual LLMs Share a Language-Agnostic Negation Operator and When Negation Typology Breaks It
Short Hypothesis: Negation is a logical operation, not a concept lookup, so it may be implemented by a language-agnostic circuit distinct from the shared 'concept space' documented for facts. We hypothesize (1) multilingual LLMs encode a compact, causally-active 'negation direction' in the residual stream that is largely shared across typologically diverse languages; (2) this shared operator is disrupted by cross-linguistic negation typology, especially negative-concord languages (Spanish 'no...nada', Russian double-marking) where a single logical negation is expressed by multiple surface markers, causing systematic double-negation / scope errors; and (3) steering along the shared negation direction can causally flip the model's affirmative/negative interpretation across languages and can repair negation-typology-induced errors.
Related Work: Prior negation work in multilingual NLP (Shaitarova & Rinaldi 2021) studies zero-shot negation-scope tagging with mBERT/XLM-R encoders, correlating results with typology but never probing internal mechanisms or causal directions in generative LLMs. Interpretability work (Wang et al. 2025, 'Lost in Multilinguality') shows facts are stored in a shared concept space transitioning to language-specific space in final layers; but this concerns concept lookup, not logical operators. General LLM negation-failure studies are almost exclusively English. No work asks whether negation itself is implemented by a shared cross-lingual circuit, whether a steerable negation direction exists, or whether negation typology (negative concord vs. single negation vs. double negation) causally interferes with that shared operator. Our proposal is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual study of negation as a language-agnostic vs. language-specific operation, with a typology-graded interference analysis and a training-free repair.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are known to store factual concepts in a largely language-agnostic space, but concepts are lookups, whereas negation is a logical operation that transforms meaning. We ask whether negation is implemented by a shared, language-agnostic circuit in multilingual LLMs, and whether the cross-linguistic diversity of how negation is expressed—single negation, double negation, and negative concord (multiple negative markers for one logical negation, as in Spanish 'no vi nada')—interferes with that circuit. Using minimally-contrasting affirmative/negative sentence pairs across ten languages spanning distinct negation typologies and scripts, we test three claims. First, we extract a 'negation direction' via difference-of-means over affirmative vs. negated activations and test whether a direction learned in one language linearly decodes negation in all others (evidence of a shared operator) and whether a single low-rank subspace captures negation across languages. Second, we measure negation-comprehension accuracy (entailment/polarity judgments, negated cloze) and test whether negative-concord and double-negation languages show systematically more scope/double-negation errors, controlling for resource level. Third, using activation patching we localize where negation is computed and where the shared operator diverges into language-specific machinery, and we test a training-free intervention that steers the shared negation direction to flip polarity and to repair typology-induced errors. Across four open models we report cross-lingual negation-probe transfer, typology-graded error patterns, causal localization, and steering-based flip and repair rates, offering a mechanistic account of negation as a partly-shared, partly-language-specific logical operator.
Experiments: 1) Stimulus construction: Build ~800 minimal affirmative/negated sentence pairs (semantics held constant, only polarity changes) plus polarity-judgment and negated-cloze items, translated into 10 languages spanning negation typologies: single-negation (English, German, Turkish, Mandarin, Swahili), negative-concord (Spanish, Italian, Russian, Hindi), and double-negation-permitting/other (French with 'ne...pas', Portuguese). Assign each language a typology label and a 'negative-marker count' feature. Verify translations via native/MT checks. 2) Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. 3) Shared-negation probe: Extract mid-layer residual activations at the sentence-final token for affirmative vs. negated versions; train a linear probe to classify polarity using ONLY one source language and evaluate zero-shot transfer to all target languages (report per-language AUC vs. in-language ceiling and chance). Do reciprocal source sweeps. Compute difference-of-means negation directions per language; measure cross-language cosine/CCA and test whether a single low-rank subspace (PCA) captures negation across languages. 4) Behavioral negation comprehension: measure accuracy on polarity-judgment / entailment (does the negated sentence contradict the affirmative?) and negated cloze; regress error rate on negation typology and negative-marker count, including a language-resource covariate, to test whether negative-concord/double-negation languages incur excess double-negation/scope errors beyond resource level. Include an English-embedded control (translate content, vary only negation structure) to isolate typology from prompt language. 5) Causal localization: use activation patching to (a) patch the negated-sentence representation into an affirmative run and test if the model's judgment flips, sweeping layers to localize where negation is computed, and (b) compare the localization/direction across languages to identify where the shared operator diverges into language-specific machinery (predict divergence in later layers, echoing concept-space findings but testing it for a logical operator). 6) Steering interventions: (a) Flip test: add/subtract the shared negation direction at the localized layer and measure the rate at which affirmative interpretations flip to negative and vice versa, per language (manipulation check for a causal shared operator). (b) Repair test: for negative-concord/double-negation languages where the model mis-handles multiple markers, steer along the shared negation direction to enforce a single logical negation and measure error reduction, with specificity controls (no degradation on single-negation languages or on non-negation control tasks) and fluency filters. 7) Ablations: layer choice, probe rank, steering strength, PCA subspace dimensionality, robustness across the four models. Metrics: cross-lingual negation-probe AUC and transfer gap, negation-direction cross-language similarity, typology-vs-error partial correlation (Spearman), patching flip/localization curves, steering flip rate, repair accuracy delta, specificity, and fluency pass rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Difference-of-means directions may entangle negation with the specific negative-marker tokens rather than the logical operation; we mitigate by using minimal pairs with varied lexical realizations, testing cross-noun/cross-construction generalization, and validating on held-out constructions. 2) Behavioral typology effects could be confounded with resource level and translation quality; we control via resource covariates, the English-embedded structural-control design, and native/MT verification. 3) A null result (negation is largely language-specific, or typology has no effect) is itself a clean, informative finding contrasting negation with the shared concept space. 4) Activation-patching localization is model-specific; we report across four models and sweep layers. 5) Polarity-judgment scoring for open-ended outputs can be noisy; we use structured yes/no or multiple-choice formats and validate a subset manually. 6) Steering may reduce fluency or over-flip; we include manipulation checks, specificity controls, and fluency filters. 7) Some languages have multiple co-existing negation strategies; we annotate the dominant construction and stratify analyses accordingly.
